marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q001.takeaway: When light enters the eye, it first traverses the inner retinal surface, including the retinal ganglion-cell layer, before reaching the photoreceptor outer segments near the choroid. The neural signal then travels in the opposite direction: photoreceptors signal through bipolar cells to ganglion cells. The retina has ten histologic layers.
marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q001.displayText: Light passes through the inner retina before reaching photoreceptors; neural signaling proceeds back toward ganglion cells.

rationales.a: The inner nuclear layer contains bipolar, horizontal, and amacrine cell bodies; it lies deeper than the ganglion-cell layer on the path light takes from the vitreous.
rationales.b: The outer nuclear layer houses photoreceptor nuclei and is reached after light has crossed inner retinal layers.
rationales.c: The outer plexiform layer is also posterior to the ganglion-cell layer, so it is not the first layer encountered.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q002.takeaway: The visual impulse begins when a photon photoisomerizes retinal in rhodopsin (visual purple). Rhodopsin is the photosensitive pigment of rods and consists of opsin, a G-protein-coupled receptor protein, plus retinal, the aldehyde form of vitamin A. Photoisomerization initiates phototransduction; it is not a vitamin-A condensation reaction.
marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q002.displayText: Photon-driven retinal photoisomerization in rhodopsin initiates phototransduction.

rationales.a: Opsin combines with 11-cis retinal to form rhodopsin, but that assembly is not the light-triggered event that initiates a visual impulse.
rationales.c: NADP is not the chromophore event in rod phototransduction; the key trigger is retinal isomerization in rhodopsin.
rationales.d: NAD is not the photosensitive pigment or the photon-driven initiating reaction.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q003.takeaway: Opsin combines with 11-cis-retinaldehyde to form rhodopsin. Retinol is a vitamin-A alcohol and must be oxidized to retinaldehyde; the 11-cis configuration is the chromophore bound to opsin. Photon absorption then isomerizes retinal and starts the visual transduction cascade.

rationales.a: All-trans retinal is produced after photon absorption and must be converted back to the 11-cis form before it can recombine with opsin.
rationales.c: All-trans retinol is the alcohol form and has the wrong isomeric form; it is not the chromophore that binds opsin.
rationales.d: 11-cis retinol has the correct cis geometry but is still an alcohol, not the retinaldehyde chromophore.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q004.takeaway: The foveola at the center of the macula is rod-free and contains only cones, supporting the highest spatial resolution. The macula lutea lies temporal to the optic disc and supports central vision with high photoreceptor density. The optic disc has no photoreceptors and creates the physiologic blind spot. Toward the peripheral retina the rod-to-cone ratio and convergence increase, improving sensitivity in dim light at the cost of acuity.

Only cones occupy the foveola; peripheral retina is rod-rich and more sensitive but less acute.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q005.takeaway: Light causes rods to hyperpolarize, unlike the depolarizing receptor potentials common in many sensory receptors. In darkness, cGMP-gated sodium channels in the outer segment remain open; the phototransduction cascade triggered by light closes these channels, reducing inward current and making the rod membrane more negative. The change in graded receptor potential alters transmitter release onto bipolar cells.

rationales.a: Depolarization is the typical response of many receptor cells to stimulation, but rods respond to light with hyperpolarization.
rationales.b: The membrane becomes more negative during the light response, rather than less negative.
rationales.c: Light closes cGMP-gated sodium channels and reduces inward sodium current; it does not increase sodium conductance.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q006.takeaway: Rods and cones are the first-order neurons of the visual pathway. They transduce photons into graded receptor potentials and signal locally to bipolar and horizontal cells. Bipolar cells relay within the retina; ganglion cells are the retinal output neurons whose axons form the optic nerve and project to central targets, including the lateral geniculate nucleus.
marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q006.displayText:
Rods and cones are first-order visual neurons; ganglion cells provide retinal output to the optic nerve.

Source explanation detail: Photoreceptors - rods and cones are the first-order neurons in the visual pathway

rationales.b: Ganglion cells are the retinal output neurons and their axons form the optic nerve; they are downstream from photoreceptors.
rationales.c: Lateral geniculate neurons are a central relay beyond the retina, not first-order retinal neurons.
rationales.d: Bipolar cells are interneurons between photoreceptors and ganglion cells, not the first-order neurons.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q007.takeaway: Retinal response polarity distinguishes these cells: rods, cones, and horizontal cells respond with hyperpolarizing potentials; bipolar-cell responses may be either hyperpolarizing or depolarizing. Amacrine cells produce purely depolarizing potentials in the source's classification. These are graded retinal responses rather than the all-or-none spiking characteristic of ganglion cells.
marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q007.displayText: Amacrine cells are the purely depolarizing retinal elements in this classification.

rationales.a: Bipolar cells may be either hyperpolarizing or depolarizing; they are not purely depolarizing.
rationales.b: Cones, like rods, have hyperpolarizing responses to light.
rationales.d: Rods hyperpolarize when illuminated; they do not show the purely depolarizing response asked about.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q008.takeaway: Amacrine cells release acetylcholine in the keyed item. They are retinal interneurons that connect bipolar-cell output with ganglion-cell dendrites and other amacrine cells within the inner plexiform layer. The source also lists GABA, glycine, dopamine, and indolamine among amacrine transmitters and notes that rods and cones release glutamate at synapses with bipolar cells; therefore transmitter identity depends on the retinal cell and synapse.
marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q008.displayText: The keyed transmitter for amacrine cells here is acetylcholine; rods and cones release glutamate to bipolar cells.

rationales.b: Serotonin is not the transmitter identified by the source for this item; it lists acetylcholine among amacrine-cell transmitters.
rationales.c: Histamine is not the keyed retinal amacrine transmitter in this source.
rationales.d: Glutamate is released by rods and cones onto bipolar cells, distinguishing those photoreceptor synapses from the keyed amacrine answer.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q009.takeaway: Ganglion cells are the only retinal neurons that generate action potentials. Photoreceptors, bipolar cells, and other retinal interneurons communicate with graded local potentials; ganglion-cell spikes carry retinal output along the optic nerve.
marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q009.displayText:
Ganglion cells are the retinal neurons that fire action potentials.

Source explanation detail: ‘All neural elements in the retina exhibit local graded potentials except ganglion cells which shows

action potential.

rationales.a: Bipolar cells use graded potentials rather than the retinal action potentials attributed to ganglion cells.
rationales.c: Amacrine cells are interneurons with local responses; they are not the retinal output cells that fire action potentials.
rationales.d: Rods and cones signal with graded receptor potentials rather than action potentials.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q010.takeaway: Each lateral geniculate nucleus receives crossed input from the contralateral nasal retina in layers 1, 4, and 6, and uncrossed input from the ipsilateral temporal retina in layers 2, 3, and 5. Because nasal-retinal fibers cross at the optic chiasm, the laminar input preserves eye-specific streams in the LGN.
marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q010.displayText: Contralateral nasal-retinal fibers terminate in LGN layers 1, 4, and 6.

rationales.a: Layers 2, 3, and 5 receive ipsilateral temporal-retinal input, not contralateral nasal-retinal input.
rationales.c: Layers 1–3 mix the two eye-specific sets and omit contralateral layers 4 and 6.
rationales.d: Layers 4–6 include layer 4 and 6 contralateral input but layer 5 is ipsilateral; the full correct set is 1, 4, and 6.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q011.takeaway: The parvocellular pathway carries color, texture, shape, fine detail, and accurate point-to-point spatial information. It receives input from type X retinal ganglion cells and projects through LGN layers 3–6. The magnocellular pathway receives type Y ganglion-cell input in LGN layers 1–2, is colorblind (black-and-white), and emphasizes movement, depth, and flicker. The source table names layer 4C for both pathways; the continuation on printed page 252 refines this: magnocellular input ends in 4Cα and parvocellular input in 4Cβ.
marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q011.displayText: Parvocellular processing carries color and fine spatial detail; magnocellular processing emphasizes movement, depth, and flicker.

rationales.b: Luminous contrast is not the feature singled out by the table; the parvocellular list centers on color and fine spatial detail.
rationales.c: Temporal frequency and flicker are emphasized by the magnocellular pathway, not the parvocellular pathway.
rationales.d: Saccadic eye movements are not the parvocellular pathway's listed function; the table assigns it color, texture, shape, and detail.
